Concepts and detection logic for failed logon detection in Splunk (high level):
- Identify authentication failure events from relevant data sources (Windows Security logon failures, Linux/Unix auth failures, application auth logs) and ensure they are normalized across sourcetypes (fields like user, src_ip, host, status or result, timestamp).
- Normalize and map fields so you can compare across platforms (e.g., user, source IP, host, event/status, and time).
- Detect abuse patterns by aggregating failures over moving time windows and by entity:
  - Spot high-rate failures for a single user or from a single source IP within a short interval.
  - Detect multiple failed attempts across many users from the same origin.
  - Look for sequences where failures precede a successful login from the same origin or after a lockout event.
- Use thresholds and baselining to distinguish brute-force attempts from legitimate activity; consider rate, diversity of targets, and time-of-day context.
- Enrich data with context (geolocation, ASN, user attributes) to prioritize investigations.
- Surface findings via dashboards or alerts that trigger on anomalous failure patterns, spikes, or cross-signal correlations (failures + lockouts, unusual login times).
- Ensure data handling adheres to privacy and security policies, and tailor detectors to your environment’s data model and available fields.
- Remember to adapt concepts to your environment’s specific data sources and field names rather than applying a one-size-fits-all SPL template.

High-level concepts for tuning a CrowdStrike Falcon prevention policy (unverified web source):
- Define policy objectives and risk tolerance: determine how aggressive the policy should be, with tighter controls on critical assets and more lenient settings on non-critical devices to reduce false positives. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Use a two-phase approach: start in detective/monitoring mode to collect signals, then gradually enable blocking for verified detections to minimize disruption. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Apply granular scope: segment devices by role, OS, and asset criticality, so stricter policies target high-value endpoints while allowing others to operate with fewer blocks. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Tune detection categories gradually: begin with non-blocking checks on malware, exploitation, script control, and memory-protection signals, then progressively enable blocks as confidence grows. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Use exception lifecycle management: implement controlled allowlisting for legitimate software or scripts, with regular review and expiration to keep protections current. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Monitor telemetry and validate coverage: track false positives and true positives, measure protection coverage across ATT&CK techniques in a high-level, non-operational way, and adjust the policy accordingly. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/data-connectors-reference)
- Coordinate with other controls: align Falcon policy with broader security controls (identity, EDR telemetry, and network controls) to avoid gaps or conflicts. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/data-connectors-reference)
- Documentation and governance: maintain change-control for policy updates and periodic reviews to reflect evolving threatlands and business needs. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)

- Look for suspicious process creation patterns, unusual parent-child relationships, or attempts to execute code from uncommon locations. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)
- Identify suspicious script or macro activity, unusual PowerShell or shell usage, and attempts to bypass controls. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/mobile-threat-defense/crowdstrike-falcon)

- Correlate with network indicators such as anomalous outbound connections or connections to known bad domains as part of broader threat signals. unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/sentinel/data-connectors-reference)

Key detection concepts for password spraying in Microsoft Sentinel (KQL concepts, not configuration steps):
- Core pattern: a rapid burst of failed sign-in attempts targeting many user accounts from a small set of IP addresses within a short time window.
- Data sources: primarily SignInLogs (Azure AD sign-in data); correlate failed sign-ins across accounts and from common IPs to identify spray activity, possibly with geolocation/time anomalies.
- Detection patterns (conceptual):
  - Burst of failed sign-ins per IP or per small set of IPs with a high count of attempts in a defined window (e.g., 1 hour).
  - High number of distinct targeted accounts from the same IP within that window.
  - Correlation with successful sign-ins to flag potential progression after spray.
- High-level KQL concept (no step-by-step config):
  - Aggregate failures by IPAddress over a rolling window to identify bursts.
  - Aggregate distinct UserPrincipalName values per IP to identify mass targeting.
  - Combine signals to raise a defensive alert when thresholds are exceeded and patterns match spray behavior.
- Tuning and context: thresholds should be tailored to the environment, and you may want to incorporate additional context (geo, time-of-day, known safe IPs) to reduce false positives.

For additional guidance and concrete examples, see these sources:
- Password spray investigation | Microsoft Learn (unverified web source) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/security-operations-playbook-password-spray

Concepts and detection logic only (no step-by-step GoDaddy navigation):

- DMARC concept: DMARC is a domain-level policy published in DNS that tells receivers how to handle messages that fail SPF and/or DKIM checks, and where to send reports about those evaluations. It helps protect against domain spoofing and phishing by specifying policy and reporting. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/email-authentication-dmarc-configure)

- Where the DMARC policy lives: Publish a TXT record in the domain’s DNS with a host/name of _dmarc (under your domain). The record value begins with v=DMARC1 and includes policy and reporting options, e.g., p=none/quarantine/reject, and optional rua (aggregate reports) and ruf (forensic reports). Alignment options (adkim and aspf) control DKIM/SPF alignment requirements. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6048218/add-a-dmarc-record-to-the-dns)

- GoDaddy or other DNS providers: The DNS hosting provider for your domain is where the _dmarc TXT record must be posted. The key concept is that the DMARC policy is a TXT record in DNS; the exact navigation will vary by provider, but the record’s host and syntax remain the same. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6048218/add-a-dmarc-record-to-the-dns)

- Detection and monitoring logic: After publishing, monitor DMARC reports (rua) to assess how mail from your domain is being evaluated by receivers. Use the reports to identify misconfigurations (e.g., DKIM not signing all legitimate mail, SPF alignment issues, or forwarded mail breaking SPF). Ensure DKIM signing is in place for all mailstreams and that SPF records include legitimate sending sources. Adjust policy gradually (e.g., p=none → p=quarantine → p=reject) as you gain confidence. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/email-authentication-dmarc-configure)

- Quick cautions for GoDaddy DNS users: If you’re using GoDaddy for DNS, DMARC is implemented by adding the same DMARC TXT record concept in their DNS zone editor. Propagation can take some time, and begin with a monitoring policy (p=none) to observe reports before enforcing stricter actions. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/6048218/add-a-dmarc-record-to-the-dns)

The CVSS v4.0 base score measures the intrinsic severity of a vulnerability based on its own characteristics (i.e., a technical severity), and it is designed to be independent of time, patch status, or environment. unverified web source (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2022/NIST.IR.8409.pdf) 

It is calculated from eight base metrics: Attack Vector (AV), Attack Complexity (AC), Privileges Required (PR), User Interaction (UI), Scope (S), and the Impact metrics for Confidentiality (C), Integrity (I), and Availability (A). unverified web source (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2022/NIST.IR.8409.pdf) 

The base score yields a numeric value from 0 to 10 and is intended to reflect the vulnerability’s severity under baseline conditions, i.e., the core exploitability and impact characteristics, without considering time or environmental factors. unverified web source (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2022/NIST.IR.8409.pdf) 

In practice, CVSS-based assessments use the base score as a starting point and combine it with Temporal and Environmental scores to represent risk in a specific context. unverified web source (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)

output_text: STIX 2.1 provides a JSON-based data model and language for describing cyber threat intelligence to support interoperability in threat-sharing. It defines a set of core object types (e.g., Indicator, Threat Actor, Intrusion Set, Campaign, Malware, Tool, Attack Pattern, Observables, Observed Data, Relationship, Identity, Marking Definition, Bundle) and how they relate via Relationship objects. Each object includes metadata (id, type, created, modified) and spec_version set to 2.1. Indicators use the STIX Patterning Language to express observable patterns. Bundles group related objects for transport, and data markings/granular markings label data provenance and sensitivity. The overall aim is to provide a consistent, machine-readable vocabulary that enables automated ingestion, correlation, and enrichment when sharing threat intelligence across organizations and tooling.

output_text: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) moves DNS queries from plain text to encrypted HTTPS traffic to a resolver, so the actual domains a host resolves are not visible in traditional network DNS logs. In DoH, the DNS query content is carried inside TLS-encrypted HTTP, so only the DoH endpoint and, to a limited extent, TLS metadata (e.g., SNI) may be visible to network devices; the domain names themselves are hidden from standard DNS visibility. This reduces the SOC’s ability to see what destinations hosts are trying to reach using conventional DNS logs.
